bigPicture: US inflation surprised on the upside: consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices 0.3%, so a Federal Reserve rate hike on 9 December now looks almost certain, and traders even see a small chance of a half-point move. That turned a global rebound into a US sell-off in tech shares, bonds and gold, while Nvidia slid again over its CEO's alleged links to a Chinese agent and Anthropic set a share-sale range valuing it at up to $1.4 trillion. Oil kept falling, with Brent briefly below $90 for the first time since August, after Trump said he would hold off on new strikes on Iran, though the US blockade stays. In Abu Dhabi, Russia, Ukraine and the US opened their first three-way talks since February as Russian strikes cut power in six Ukrainian regions. UNICEF warned that drones now cause two in three child casualties in Sudan's war.

stories.title: US inflation comes in hotter than expected (+0.4% in October), and a Fed rate hike in December now looks almost certain
stories.what: The US consumer price index (CPI, the price of a typical basket of goods and services) rose 0.4% in October from September, after seasonal adjustment, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists had expected 0.3%. 'Core' prices, which leave out volatile food and energy, rose 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast, the same pace as in August and September. Food rose 0.5%, energy 0.7% (after a 5.2% jump in September) and shelter 0.3%. No year-on-year figure was published for most items, because October 2025 prices were never collected during last year's government shutdown.
stories.why: The Federal Reserve (the US central bank) left its key rate at 3.75%–4.00% in October and has signalled further tightening; a third straight month of 0.3% core inflation strengthens the case for raising it on 8–9 December. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would back at least a quarter-point hike and that a half-point move should be considered if core prices rose 0.3% or more, which they did. After the data, futures traders priced roughly an 84% chance of a quarter-point hike and about 15% of a half-point hike, according to Yahoo Finance's report of CME FedWatch.

stories.title: Trump says he will hold off on new strikes against Iran but keeps the naval blockade; Brent oil slips below $90 for the first time since August
stories.what: After meeting Qatar's prime minister, President Donald Trump said further US military action against Iran did not now seem necessary and that he was holding off on new strikes after appeals from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait; he said US forces stay ready to resume if needed. The US naval blockade of Iranian ports continues. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Tehran's own proposal (US ends the blockade, lifts some sanctions and stops strikes; Iran ends its shipping restrictions in Hormuz), which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called unrealistic. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dipped below $90 a barrel for the first time since August before recovering to about $90.3, while US WTI crude traded near $84.8, down about 2.3%.
stories.why: Traders expect that an end to the fighting would eventually free up Gulf oil supply, so prices fall on hopes of de-escalation, The National reported. But the blockade and Iran's restrictions in Hormuz remain, and attacks on tankers in the Gulf rose sharply in October, so supply is still disrupted. Saudi forces also shot down Houthi missiles over Riyadh on Tuesday, a reminder that the conflict is spreading around the region.

stories.title: Russia, Ukraine and the US hold their first three-way talks since February in Abu Dhabi as Russia strikes Ukraine's power grid again
stories.what: Delegations led by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukraine's Rustem Umerov and Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky opened two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first three-way meeting since February. Kushner said recent contacts had 'narrowed the gaps'; Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Moscow would not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what comes next. Security guarantees for Ukraine are the main topic. Overnight, Russian air attacks hit 10 Ukrainian regions and five major electrical substations, killing two people in Vinnytsia region and cutting power in six regions including Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipropetrovsk, according to Reuters reporting and the grid operator Ukrenergo.
stories.why: Both sides are tired after almost five years of full-scale war, Trump said, and an anonymous US official told Al Jazeera both sides had privately shown some flexibility on territory. But the positions remain far apart: Ukraine wants a ceasefire first and refuses to give up land Russia has not captured, while Russia wants all of the Donbas region. Strikes on the power grid before winter add pressure on Ukraine's civilians.

stories.title: Wall Street, gold and bonds fall after the inflation surprise; Nvidia slides again over its CEO's alleged links to a Chinese agent
stories.what: By early afternoon in New York the S&P 500 was down about 0.9% at roughly 7,482 and the Nasdaq about 1.5% lower, according to Yahoo Finance quotes at about 13:05 New York time (19:05 Warsaw). The US 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.93%–4.95%, up 7 to 9 basis points (sources differ slightly). Gold fell around 2% to roughly $4,050 an ounce and Bitcoin briefly dipped below $73,000. Nvidia fell about 6% by midday after The Information reported that CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a businesswoman accused of spying for Beijing helped at least $7.5 billion of its chips reach Chinese firms; Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation and a shareholder class action was filed in San Jose. Hims & Hers fell as much as 15% after a weak revenue forecast.
stories.why: Higher expected US interest rates make future company profits worth less today and make interest-paying bonds more attractive, so expensive tech shares are hit hardest (lesson 7 and 8). Gold pays no interest, so it tends to lose appeal when rates and the dollar rise. Europe had closed before the worst of the US slide: the DAX ended about 0.3%–0.5% higher after giving back most of its morning gains, which sources attributed to the US data.

stories.title: AI company Anthropic sets its share-sale price range, implying a value of up to about $1.4 trillion
stories.what: Anthropic, the US artificial-intelligence company that makes the Claude models, said in an updated filing that it plans to sell 825 million new shares at $70 to $78 each, raising about $57.8–64.4 billion. At the top of the range it would be valued at about $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis (counting all shares that could exist), well above the $965 billion of its May funding round. It also agreed to sell $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. The filing shows nine-month revenue of $33.2 billion and a nine-month net loss of $104 billion; trading on Nasdaq under the ticker 'ANT' is expected around 19 November, CNBC reported.
stories.why: An initial public offering (IPO) is when a private company first sells shares to the public; the price range is the company's and its banks' estimate of what investors will pay. Very large losses alongside fast-growing revenue reflect huge spending on computing power, with $900.9 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments disclosed, according to TechCrunch. The size of the offering means its reception will be read as a signal for the whole AI sector, which fell sharply last week.

stories.title: UNICEF: armed drones caused two in three child casualties in Sudan this year, as strikes on power stations cut water supplies
stories.what: The UN children's agency UNICEF said on Tuesday that armed drones were responsible for two in three child casualties in Sudan this year, with some drones travelling up to 1,500 km to their targets. Up to 15 power stations were hit in October, and in the last week of the month a power station was struck every day, which stops water pumps and treatment. An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition this year, and well over 15 million people urgently need shelter. UNICEF's Sudan response is only one-third funded.
stories.why: Sudan's war has shifted toward long-range drone strikes on infrastructure, UN News reported. Without power, water systems fail, which spreads diseases such as cholera (already found in pockets of the country) and worsens malnutrition alongside drought.

stories.title: China extends its pause on tough rare-earth and battery export controls until 10 January 2027, keeping the US–China trade truce alive
stories.what: China's Ministry of Commerce said it will keep suspending a package of export controls first announced in October 2025, which was due to lapse on 10 November; the pause now runs to 10 January 2027. The suspended rules cover rare-earth equipment and technology, high-end lithium battery materials, graphite anodes and industrial synthetic diamonds, plus a rule that would have required licences for foreign-made goods containing even 0.1% (by value) of Chinese-origin rare earths. China's separate licensing system for seven heavy rare earths, in force since April 2025, stays in place. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the broader truce runs to 10 January 2027.
stories.why: Rare earths are metals used in powerful magnets for motors and electronics; China mined about 60% of those used in magnets in 2024 and handled about 91% of separation and refining, figures originally from the International Energy Agency cited by Tech Times. Keeping the pause avoids a supply shock for manufacturers while Washington and Beijing negotiate; Trump is expected to meet Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month. US officials told the Financial Times that China has met about two-thirds of its rare-earth commitments, which Beijing disputes.

stories.title: Poland's defence minister says the Pentagon has given a 'green light' to a permanent US base; the White House is to decide in early December
stories.what: After meeting US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington, Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland interprets Hegseth's answer as a green light from the Pentagon for a permanent US military base in Poland. He stressed that the final decision rests with the White House and is expected in early December. On Tuesday the two sides also agreed on a service and certification centre in Poland for PAC-3 MSE missiles (used in Patriot air-defence systems), which would be the only one outside the United States; missile production would need further talks. The US is reviewing its military presence in Europe, with the review due to end in late 2026.
stories.why: Warsaw wants to lock in US forces before the review concludes, as some units could be moved from Germany, Italy and Spain toward NATO's eastern flank, Rzeczpospolita reported. A permanent base signals a longer commitment than rotating troops.

stories.title: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal: rival orders as judges meet again and the Tribunal's president insists only his instructions are valid
stories.what: Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on 30 October suspended Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański for a month citing a non-executed interim measure of the European Court of Human Rights, convened another General Assembly of judges for 10 November, where judges chosen by the current Sejm are working on changes to the Tribunal's rules. The same day Święczkowski issued an order stating that only instructions from the president or vice-president bind judges and staff and that acts of 'unauthorised' persons have no legal effect. He says police do not let him onto the Tribunal's grounds. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would publish the assembly's resolution in the official journal.
stories.why: The dispute stems from years of conflict over how Tribunal judges were appointed; each side considers the other's decisions invalid, so the government's choice of which rulings to publish becomes decisive, WP reported.

stories.title: Nearly 64,000 people have fled violence in northern Nigeria to Niger this year, the UN refugee agency says
stories.what: UNHCR said on Tuesday that nearly 64,000 people have fled northern Nigeria to Niger in 2026, escaping attacks by Islamist militants and armed gangs, Reuters reported. Niger already hosts more than 500,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, about 327,500 of them Nigerians. More than 23,000 people, over two-thirds of them children, have reached Niger's Diffa region since January, and only about 5% of this year's arrivals have been formally registered. UNHCR is seeking $11.4 million for its response in Niger, Nigeria and Benin.
stories.why: Attacks by Boko Haram, ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province) fighters and criminal gangs have displaced millions in northern Nigeria over the past decade. Aid agencies report rising malnutrition, respiratory infections and poor sanitation among new arrivals, who have little access to food, water and shelter, UNHCR spokesperson Dominique Hyde said.

stories.everyday: Budget squeezes are felt first in public services like schools; Poland faces similar debates over teacher pay and deficits.
stories.rankWhy: A nationwide education strike in the EU's second-largest economy reflects a wider fight over the 2027 budget and public-sector pay.

sources.name: Sortiraparis – Education strike and student protest, 10 November
France 24 – French PM presents belt-tightening 2027 budget

stories.title: French teachers, university staff and students strike again over pay, staffing and planned research job cuts
stories.what: Fifteen unions and student organisations called a nationwide education strike and marches on Tuesday, following a 5 November strike when the main secondary teachers' union Snes-FSU said 52% of staff walked out and authorities counted nearly 600,000 marchers (the CGT union said 1.6 million). Demands include unfreezing the public-sector pay index, hiring more teachers, nurses and psychologists, 150,000 more university places and scrapping job cuts in research planned in the 2027 budget. The government has offered a €5 billion plan for high schools and universities and smaller classes, which the unions say falls short.
stories.why: France is trying to cut its budget deficit with frozen wages and new taxes in the 2027 budget, according to France 24, which collides with demands for more spending on schools. The movement began in mid-September at a high school near Paris over vacant posts.

stories.everyday: Impeachment by the House would not by itself remove Hegseth: removal requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate after a trial.
stories.rankWhy: A first House vote on impeaching the US defence secretary over the Iran war tests support for the war inside the president's own party.

sources.name: ABC News – Hegseth blasts impeachment effort
WLKY – House schedules procedural vote on Massie's effort
The Tribune – Massie says resolution to face House vote

stories.title: US House to hold a first vote on a Republican's articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Hegseth over the Iran war
stories.what: Republican Representative Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, accusing him of violating the Constitution and federal law, including by conducting military operations in Iran without congressional authorisation and through strikes in Yemen, Venezuela and on boats suspected of carrying drugs. The House scheduled a procedural motion on the resolution for Tuesday at 17:30 Washington time (23:30 Warsaw), which could send it to committee or block it; if it survives, a debate and vote on the articles would follow. Hegseth called the effort a 'political spectacle', and President Trump defended him.
stories.why: Impeachment resolutions are 'privileged', so House leaders must act within two legislative days, forcing members to go on record, ABC News reported. Several Republicans have blamed their party's midterm losses on the Iran war.

stories.everyday: Polish firms exporting to the EU already deal with the EU's climate rules; CBAM puts a carbon price on some imports into the EU.
stories.rankWhy: How much rich countries pay to help poorer ones cut emissions and adapt shapes climate action for billions of people, but no decision was taken today.

sources.name: Business Standard – COP31 opens with climate finance clash
Infocons – COP31 energy and transport day, 10 November

stories.title: COP31: rich and developing countries clash over climate finance as the Antalya talks start, with few leaders confirmed for Wednesday's summit
stories.what: Disagreement over whether to put a work programme on climate finance on the agenda delayed the opening of the UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, by more than an hour, Business Standard reported. The EU and the 'Umbrella Group' (including Australia, Canada and the UK) resisted, while the G77 group of developing countries and China pushed for it; EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra called new finance demands 'dead in the water'. The current goal, agreed at COP29 in Baku in 2024, is at least $300 billion a year by 2035; the OECD counted $136.7 billion of public climate finance to developing countries last year. Tuesday's themed day focused on energy and transport.
stories.why: Developing countries argue that those who emitted most historically should pay most, while donor governments face tight budgets; trade measures such as the EU's carbon border levy (CBAM) are another sore point.

stories.everyday: Most direct effect is on border guards, police and other officials; the nuclear and deregulation measures aim at lower costs for businesses over time.
stories.rankWhy: Changes Polish criminal law on migrant smuggling and attacks on officials, plus rules for shipping and nuclear-plant construction.

sources.name: Gov.pl – Komunikaty CIR (10 Nov 2026)

stories.title: Polish government adopts a bill raising penalties for attacks on officials and for organising illegal border crossings
stories.what: Poland's Council of Ministers adopted a bill that increases penalties for attacks on public officials and for organising illegal border crossings, including for people who smuggle migrants for profit and endanger their lives or cause their deaths, the Prime Minister's Chancellery said. The government also approved a single digital ship register to make registering ships under the Polish flag easier, simplified procedures for preparing and building nuclear power plants, and a 'planned deregulation' programme to cut red tape for businesses. The bill still has to pass parliament.
stories.why: Government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said the law tightens criminal liability; the stated aim is to protect officials and border security, and to deter smugglers who put migrants' lives at risk.

stories.everyday: Many Polish pension and investment funds hold Allegro; for shoppers, its results show how Polish online spending is growing.
stories.rankWhy: Allegro is Poland's largest e-commerce platform and one of the biggest companies on the WIG20.

sources.name: Investing.com/ISBnews – WIG20 rose 1.04% on Tuesday
Investing.com – Allegro shares up 17% before results

stories.title: Warsaw shares rise before the holiday; Allegro reaches a 52-week high ahead of Thursday's results
stories.what: The WIG20 index of Warsaw's largest companies rose 1.04% to 4,208.46 points, with turnover of about 3.39 billion złoty, the most of it in Allegro, ISBnews reported. Allegro shares traded around 61 złoty in the afternoon, a new 52-week high, almost 18% above their level a month earlier and roughly 96% up this year, Investing.com reported. The company publishes third-quarter results on Thursday 12 November before the market opens; the Warsaw exchange is closed on Wednesday for Independence Day.
stories.why: Investors expect the results to confirm Allegro's raised 2026 guidance (revenue growth of 14–16%); analysts quoted by Investing.com warn that the price has already reached some targets, so even good results could trigger profit-taking.

stories.everyday: Fact-checkers help readers anywhere judge information; their arrest makes reliable news harder to get.
stories.rankWhy: Press freedom in the Arab world's most populous country affects what tens of millions can learn about their government.

sources.name: Yahoo News (Reuters) – UN rights office voices alarm on Egypt press freedom
UN Geneva press briefing, 10 Nov 2026

stories.title: UN human rights office raises alarm over Egypt's crackdown on journalists and calls for a fact-checking newsroom's release
stories.what: The UN human rights office (OHCHR) said it was alarmed by Egypt's growing crackdown on press freedom and called for the release of all six journalists of the fact-checking outlet Matsaddash, the whole newsroom, who were arrested in September and accused of spreading misinformation for the banned Muslim Brotherhood, which the outlet denies. Last month a court convicted the editor-in-chief of the independent site Mada Masr of operating without a licence and ordered the site closed. The report carried no response from Egyptian authorities.
stories.why: OHCHR spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said the Matsaddash reporters should be freed and charges arising from their legitimate journalistic work dropped.

stories.everyday: Travellers from Poland to Spain on Wednesday should check flights and trains.
stories.rankWhy: A 24-hour general strike will disrupt transport, schools and health services across Spain tomorrow.

sources.name: The Olive Press – Spain general strike: what you need to know

stories.title: Spain prepares for a 24-hour general strike on Wednesday over housing, wages and working conditions
stories.what: A nationwide 24-hour general strike begins at midnight on Wednesday 11 November, covering public and private services, with more than 4,500 union branches and works councils backing it according to the CCOO union, The Olive Press reported. Minimum services are set by region: for example, Renfe commuter trains run at 75% at peak hours, Madrid hospitals keep 35% of usual staff, and airports stay open though some flights may be cancelled. Emergency services continue.
stories.why: Housing costs, wages and working conditions are the main grievances; how many workers actually join is unclear.

stories.everyday: Relevant for Poles travelling to tropical regions where the virus spreads.
stories.rankWhy: Chikungunya has been found in more than 110 countries; long-lasting protection from one dose would matter for travellers and outbreak control.

sources.name: Valneva press release (GlobeNewswire)

stories.title: Single-dose chikungunya vaccine still protects 94% of trial adults five years on, maker Valneva reports
stories.what: French vaccine maker Valneva said 94% of 221 healthy adults evaluable five years after one dose of its chikungunya vaccine IXCHIQ still had antibody levels above the threshold agreed with regulators, with similar results in people over 65. Participants will be followed for up to ten years. Brazil's health ministry and Instituto Butantan vaccinated nearly 80,000 adults in a pilot campaign from February to October 2026.
stories.why: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus causing fever and long-lasting joint pain; more than 3.7 million cases were reported in the Americas between 2013 and 2023, according to the company. Durable antibodies could reduce the need for boosters. These are company-reported trial results, not an independent review.

stories.everyday: Memory-chip prices feed into the cost of phones, laptops and servers.
stories.rankWhy: Samsung and SK hynix are among the world's biggest memory-chip makers and dominate South Korea's market.

sources.name: Seoul Economic Daily – KOSPI rebounds 4.4%

stories.title: Korean chip stocks rebound, but Morgan Stanley slashes its targets for Samsung and SK hynix
stories.what: Samsung Electronics rose 4.74% and SK hynix 6.69% on Tuesday as the Kospi gained 4.39%, but both had fallen 16–20% the previous week, Seoul Economic Daily reported. Morgan Stanley cut its price target for Samsung by 19% (to 309,000 won) and for SK hynix by 38% (to 1.6 million won). Foreign investors were net buyers for the first time in eight sessions, after selling about 12.58 trillion won since 30 October.
stories.why: Morgan Stanley cited expanding chip supply and possibly slower AI data-centre construction and flagged a possible earnings slump after 2028, according to the paper; analysts warned the rebound may not last.

stories.everyday: Little direct effect in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A major religious event for Argentina's Catholics with little measurable effect beyond.

sources.name: GV Wire (AP) – Pope Leo draws 650,000 in another strong Argentine turnout

stories.title: Pope Leo XIV draws a crowd reported at 650,000 to a Mass in Córdoba, Argentina
stories.what: Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass at a military airfield in Córdoba, Argentina's second-largest city, where the crowd was reported at 650,000, GV Wire reported (it did not say who made the estimate). In his sermon he praised Argentina's saints, including Mama Antula, its first woman saint. On Sunday he had urged President Javier Milei not to target the poorest with austerity cuts. The 12-day trip runs to 17 November and also includes Uruguay and Peru.
stories.why: The visit takes him to the homeland of his predecessor Francis, and his comments on austerity touch a central political debate in Argentina.

stories.everyday: May eventually affect streaming prices and bundles.
stories.rankWhy: Matters mainly to investors in the newly merged Paramount–Warner Bros. media group.

TheStreet – Stock Market Today Nov 10

stories.title: Skydance shares fall more than 8% after its first results since merging with Warner Bros. Discovery
stories.what: Shares of media company Skydance fell more than 8% after third-quarter results came in below expectations, TheWrap reported. The company targets at least $6 billion of cost savings and a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle in early 2027, but analysts cited integration risk and net debt of nearly $80 billion.
stories.why: Investors want full combined financial figures including Warner Bros. Discovery, which analysts say will come only before the fourth-quarter report.

stories.rankWhy: Affects shareholders of one large North American waste-management company.

Waste Dive – GFL sets Nov 9 deadline for take-private offers

stories.title: GFL Environmental's board rejects a $22 billion take-private proposal; shares drop
stories.what: Canadian waste company GFL Environmental's board unanimously rejected a $22 billion proposal to take it private, and its shares fell about 9% in morning trading, TheStreet reported. A special committee of independent directors had set 9 November as the deadline for final offers, Waste Dive reported.
stories.why: Taking a company private means a buyer (often a private-equity firm) purchases all its listed shares; the stock had been supported by hopes of such a deal.

stories.everyday: Shared rivers mean upstream pollution or water use affects people downstream in other countries, which is why such rules matter.
stories.rankWhy: A diplomatic push on shared rivers and lakes, with little immediate effect.

sources.name: UN Geneva press briefing, 10 Nov 2026

stories.title: UN calls for 100 countries to join the global Water Convention by 2030, a month before the UN Water Conference
stories.what: The UN Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) used Tuesday's Geneva briefing to call for 100 parties to the UN Water Convention by 2030, one month before the UN Water Conference. The convention sets rules for countries that share rivers, lakes and groundwater.
stories.why: Most of the world's fresh water crosses borders, so cooperation treaties help prevent disputes as droughts and demand grow.
